title: Hanuman's counsel
hook: to comfort Sita, the monkey who just crossed an ocean tells her he's the weakest of Sugriva's army

segments.voice: Yesterday: her doubt, part two. You're so small, Sita said, and then, even when he grew like a mountain, she said no, for reasons of safety, choice and Rama's honor. Did you name what the slower way protects? Today, Hanuman's counsel. Day six hundred twenty-four.

When you visit someone in the hospital, the hardest moment is often the goodbye. You're leaving, and they're staying, and you want to say something that will last after the door closes. Hanuman has to leave Sita in the grove. She's chosen to wait for Rama. Before he goes, she gives him tokens to take back, and he gives her something too: his counsel. A few sentences meant to hold her up until help arrives.
screen: `THE HARDEST PART IS THE GOODBYE.` → `TOKENS FOR RAMA.` → `COUNSEL FOR SITA.`

segments.voice: First, Sita's tokens. She tells Hanuman a private memory only Rama would know: a day at Chitrakuta when a crow kept attacking her, and Rama, angry, sent a single blade of grass after it, charged with divine power, and the crow found no shelter anywhere until it came back and fell at Rama's feet. Tell him that, she says, and he'll know you met me. Then she unties a jewel from her hair, the chudamani, and gives it to him. And she says it plainly: I can only hold on for a month. Then Hanuman counsels her. Don't grieve, he says. Rama and Lakshmana will come soon, with Sugriva's army, and they will burn Lanka and take you home. And then, because Sita has asked how monkeys could ever cross this ocean, he says something surprising. There are many in Sugriva's army stronger than me, he tells her, and none weaker. If I could cross, how much more easily can they? Think about that. The monkey who leapt a hundred yojanas, fought Simhika and talked his way past Surasa, calls himself the least of the army. Is it true? The story has shown us his strength; it's hard to believe. But that's not the point of the counsel. The point is what Sita needs to hear. If Hanuman is the strongest, then the rescue depends on one monkey. If he's the weakest, then help is enormous, and coming. He makes himself small, again, so that her hope can be large. That's his counsel: not just comforting words, but words shaped to what she most fears.
screen: `THE CROW AND THE BLADE OF GRASS.` · `THE JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` · `DON'T GRIEVE; RAMA WILL COME.` · then, large: `NONE IN THE ARMY IS WEAKER THAN ME.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone who's waiting for something hard: a diagnosis, a verdict, a return. What do they most fear? Hold that gently. Then let a few words of comfort form in your mind, shaped not to what you want to say, but to that fear. Keep them simple and true. Breathe them in and out, slowly, until they feel right. The bell holds the time.
Hanuman's counsel. His words to Sita before leaving: don't grieve, Rama will come, and there are many in the army stronger than me, and none weaker.
Your line: Hanuman's counsel. Today, comfort someone by answering the fear they actually have, not the one you'd guess. Day six hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: The chudamani, Sita's hair jewel, is a familiar element in Ramayana art and storytelling, and Hanuman's words of reassurance to Sita are often recited by devotees as words of comfort in hard times.

fork.setup: you're Hanuman. Sita fears no army could cross this sea. you just did it alone. what do you tell her?
options: only I could do it, so it's hopeless.
many in the army are stronger than me, and none weaker.
fork.reveal: Hanuman calls himself the least of Sugriva's army, so that Sita sees the rescue as certain, not a one-monkey miracle.

original.note: Sanskrit cūḍāmaṇi, crest jewel: cūḍā, the crown of the head, and maṇi, jewel.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hanuman's counsel is just 'don't worry'.
what it means: he shapes his words to Sita's fear, even making himself the least of the army.
what a scholar hears: Sita's crow story (the kākāsura episode) is a private memory that works as a recognition token, a device the epic uses alongside the physical tokens of ring and jewel.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 38 (the crow at Chitrakuta; the chudamani; one month)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 39 (Hanuman reassures Sita; none weaker than me)

notes: Crow story details: the crow is identified in some tellings as Indra's son (Jayanta / Kakasura); the script avoids naming him and omits the loss of the crow's eye. Confirm.
Sita's 'one month' (that she will live only a month more): confirm Sundara 38.
Hanuman's statement that there are many stronger and none weaker than him in Sugriva's army: confirm (Sundara 39).

Title note: 'Hanuman's counsel' is read here as his counsel to Sita (day 624) and his own counsel with himself (day 625); his counsel to Ravana (Sundara 51) falls in 'the fight' (day 627). A Keeper may prefer a different split.
